keyFindings.text: `db-open-close` is the one file whose *purpose* is contention: its second test holds the graph writer lock for 500 ms in one child and starts a second child with `DEEP_LOOP_WRITER_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_MS=0`, then asserts the second exits 2 with `DB_ERROR`. That test needs the lock to itself, and cut 5 already gave each file its own coverage database and lock path, so the requirement is exclusivity on one file's lock rather than on the machine. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/lifecycle/db-open-close.vitest.ts:70]`

`fanout-run` has no assertion that bounds elapsed wall time. Its timing-flavoured assertions are string ordering (`indexOf` comparisons), lower bounds (`slotDurationMs > 0`, `completedSlotMs >= 4_200`) and a `waitForFile` poll cap of 5000 ms; the only child bound is one spawn at 30 000 ms. Lower bounds cannot fail under load, so this file's 171 tests do not need a quiet machine to stay green. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/fanout-run.vitest.ts:472]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/fanout-run.vitest.ts:2540]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/fanout-run.vitest.ts:5112]`

`postflip-fanout` carries no timing bound at all: it drives the ledger and gateway through `execFileSync` and asserts state transitions. Its serial placement is not backed by any assertion this iteration could find. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/integration/deep-research-postflip-fanout.vitest.ts:1]`

Only four files carry a load-sensitive upper bound on a child process, and those are the ones whose serial placement a timing assertion justifies: `cli-codex` bounds a spawned shim at 1000 ms, `stress/fanout` bounds its runs at 12 000 ms, `lineage-timestamp-window` bounds a child at 60 000 ms (raised from 15 s by cut 5), and `db-open-close` waits at most 1000 ms for the writer lock to appear. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/stress/cli-adapter/cli-codex.vitest.ts:112]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/stress/cli-adapter/fanout.vitest.ts:118]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/lineage-timestamp-window.vitest.ts:128]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/lifecycle/db-open-close.vitest.ts:31]`

The arithmetic of moving the two unbound files into the parallel project is favourable and testable: the serial group falls from about 265 s to about 108 s, while `fanout-run` and `postflip-fanout` join a parallel group already near 240 s, so the suite's floor becomes roughly 240 s plus 108 s, near 348 s instead of 504-511 s. This is an estimate and must be measured, because the parallel group may stretch when 157 s of spawning work joins it. `[INFERENCE: from findings 1, 4, 5 and 6 plus the 504-511 s and 265 s figures in the research topic]`

The packet's own pre-cut profile measured `fanout-run` at 157 s, the slowest file in the suite, which makes it the single largest block inside the 265 s serial group. `[SOURCE: specs/system-speckit/runtime-and-release/006-test-cycle-speed/001-five-cuts/spec.md:59]`

keyFindings.text: `singleWriterReadCache` is a per-process memo of one verified scan. A hit returns the memoized head and events without re-taking the lock; a miss takes the lock, scans, and memoizes. Every append nulls the memo, because the append changed the verified head. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/authorized-ledger/append-only-ledger.ts:389]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/authorized-ledger/append-only-ledger.ts:516]`

keyFindings.text: `--maxWorkers=4` is the cheap CI proxy. Neither config pins `maxWorkers`, and Vitest accepts it as a CLI flag, so one four-worker run on this Mac predicts the `ubuntu-latest` wall without provisioning a runner. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/vitest.config.ts:26]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/vitest.config.ts:45]`

Both suites run on `ubuntu-latest`, not on a self-hosted runner: `spec-kit-check` has a 51-minute job timeout and `deep-loop-runtime` a 34-minute one, and neither declares a shard matrix. `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:95]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:98]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/deep-loop-runtime.yml:45]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/deep-loop-runtime.yml:47]`

CI already runs the `cli` lane the way `run-cli-tests.sh` does — `upgrade-legacy.vitest.ts` in one background process and every other cli file in a second, joined with `wait`. So splitting that file into shards is a test-file change inside the existing process, not a CI workflow change. `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:148]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:153]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:155]`

The core lane's parallel efficiency is poor: its summed work is roughly 302 s of import plus its test time against a 348-399 s wall, which is about 1.3-1.4× even counting the test time generously, and close to 1.0× if the import figure and the wall belong to the same run. At that efficiency a four-core runner would cost about the same wall time, not more. This is an inference and needs one instrumented run, because iteration 3 found the packet's two import figures are not comparable. `[INFERENCE: from spec.md's 338 s import and implementation-summary's 302 s import, the 348-399 s core-lane wall, and the 18-worker default]`

The deep-loop suite's 265 s serial group is the one cost that is identical on eighteen cores and on four, because it never uses more than one worker. That makes shrinking it the highest-value cut for a smaller runner, and it is the same cut iteration 2 identified from the assertion side. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/vitest.config.ts:13]`

The ranking that follows is: first shrink the serial group, because it is core-count independent; second split the heavy files, because it shortens the critical path on every runner; third cut summed import work, which is worth about 17 s on eighteen cores and only becomes material when cores are scarce; fourth the ledger caching, which iteration 4 showed buys nothing on the append path. `[INFERENCE: from findings 1-5 and iteration 4's finding 4]`

Because both components scale with the number of tests rather than with a few heavy ones, sharding divides them both: N shards, each with its own sandbox, put roughly 1/N of the calls and 1/N of the resets on each worker, and the only new cost is N sandbox copies instead of one. `[INFERENCE: from findings 1-4 and the 35.8 MB copy measured in iteration 1]`

keyFindings.text: A split has to preserve the guarantee `run-cli-tests.sh`'s header states: the first process names the exact path, so a rename fails instead of silently passing. A glob replacement would lose that unless the command asserts a non-empty match. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-cli-tests.sh:3]`

Four live lines hardcode the file: `run-cli-tests.sh` runs it as the first background process and excludes it from the second, and `spec-kit-check.yml` repeats both lines. Two feature-catalog documents also name it, but they are prose. A rename or split must update the exclude, or the second process would collect the shards and run them a second time. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-cli-tests.sh:7]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-cli-tests.sh:9]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:153]` `[SOURCE: .github/workflows/spec-kit-check.yml:155]`

Native `--shard` distributes test files, not tests, so it cannot divide a single 400 s file. Sharding the cli lane with it would spread the other 202 files while the one heavy file stayed whole on one shard. `[INFERENCE: from run-tests-sharded.mjs passing --shard through to run-tests.mjs, which forwards to vitest run]`

That runner runs its shards one at a time on purpose, and its header says why: running them together contends for the same temporary directories and databases and produces failures that belong to the harness. That is a recorded precedent for this repository, and it is the same hazard the deep-loop serial group exists to avoid. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-tests-sharded.mjs:9]`

The repository already ships a sharded runner: `npm run test:sharded` calls `scripts/run-tests-sharded.mjs`, which defaults to twelve shards and passes Vitest's native `--shard=N/M`. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-tests-sharded.mjs:15]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/scripts/run-tests-sharded.mjs:31]`

`fanout-run.vitest.ts` is 44 top-level `describe` blocks holding 171 tests, with exactly one hook: an `afterEach` that clears two module-level arrays of temp directories and hermetic environments. There is no `beforeAll`, no shared fixture, no `require.cache` manipulation, no global stubbing and no `process.env` mutation. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/fanout-run.vitest.ts:49]` `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/fanout-run.vitest.ts:519]`

ruledOutDirections.text: **Cutting node startup.** Measured at 0.020 s per start, so even eliminating every spawn saves seconds, not minutes. `[SOURCE: measured: /usr/bin/time -p node -e ""]`

**Merging `validate.sh`'s freshness check into the orchestrator.** It would save one 20 ms process per validation while changing a guard that fails closed on a stale build; not worth the risk for seconds.

**Removing the second validation pass.** It is the proof that a repair worked; removing it would drop an assertion the file exists to make. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/spec/upgrade-legacy.mjs:1190]`
**Shrinking the sandbox copy.** The payload is 35.8 MB of 3115 files, paid once in `beforeAll`, so it cannot explain a 400 s file.

No checked-in timing profile for the cli lane was found in the packet or the skill tree, so the per-test split of the 400 s is not yet known. A profile is the next evidence needed before any saving is claimed. `[SOURCE: fd -e json 'profile|timing|slow' .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime → no results]`
**Merging the seven 7-line stress wrappers into one file.** It would change which `describe` a failure is reported under and save no measurable time; the wrappers are cheap.

**Removing `db-open-close` from the serial set.** Its second test exists to make two writers contend for one lock; parallel neighbours would make the race uncontrolled rather than asserted. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/lifecycle/db-open-close.vitest.ts:70]`

**Removing `lineage-timestamp-window` from the serial set.** It bounds a child at 60 s and was already raised once for load; it is the clearest genuine timing dependency in the group. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/tests/unit/lineage-timestamp-window.vitest.ts:128]`

**Treating "it spawns children" as a reason to stay serial.** Parallel workers spawn children normally; only an upper bound on the child's duration is threatened by load, and three of the six files have none.

No record exists of *which* files failed when every file ran in parallel, so the current twelve-file set cannot be justified file by file from the packet. The blanket set was a precaution taken before the per-file evidence existed. `[SOURCE: specs/system-speckit/runtime-and-release/006-test-cycle-speed/001-five-cuts/implementation-summary.md:83]`
**Blaming one pathological import graph.** The largest graph is 747 KB over 38 modules, and the median file is 46 KB, so there is no outlier to fix.

**Cutting import time as a wall-clock lever.** At 18 workers the summed figure is a small fraction of the lane's wall; the critical path is the heavy tail. `[SOURCE: measured: os.availableParallelism() = 18]`
**Raising `maxWorkers`.** It is already unbounded and resolves to the core count; raising it past 18 would oversubscribe a machine that also runs child processes.

**Turning on `isolate: false` to make imports free.** It would cut the summed import figure but share module state across 129 files, which trades a measured metric for unmeasured flakiness and changes what each test proves.
No per-file timing exists for the core lane in the packet, so finding 5 rests on the pre-cut profile's three numbers plus worker arithmetic rather than a current measurement.
**Blaming fsync for the ledger tests' time.** The fsync is one `appendFileSync` per event; the double process and the 79-module load happen once per invocation and dominate a short test.

**Enabling `singleWriterReadCache` in the gateway.** One append per process plus a nulled memo on append leaves nothing to reuse. `[SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/authorized-ledger/append-only-ledger.ts:516]`
**Extending the cache across appends.** A memo that survives an append would let a reader return a head another writer already advanced, which is the durability contract the ledger exists to enforce.
**Treating the caching idea as unbuilt work.** It is built, has its own test, and is enabled where a process reads repeatedly.
No compiled `dist/` exists for the deep-loop runtime, so there is no cheap alternative to tsx loading today; building one is a packaging change, not a test change, and is out of this packet's scope.
**A CI shard matrix as the first move.** Both jobs already fit inside their timeouts, and sharding multiplies setup and build cost before any file gets faster.
**Optimising for the 18-core Mac.** The measured machine is not the machine that gates merges; a cut that only pays at 18 workers is a local convenience.
**Treating summed import work as the small-runner lever.** It becomes material only below a handful of cores, and the serial group dominates before that point.
No CI timing history is checked in, so the `ubuntu-latest` wall for either suite is unknown; the four-worker proxy is the only way to estimate it from this repository.
**`describe.concurrent` inside one file.** The tests share one sandbox by construction, so concurrency inside the file would make the shared baseline the assertion.
**Cutting individual heavy tests.** The top ten are 36% of the calls, so even removing them entirely would not halve the file, and removing tests is out of scope.
**Raising the 180 s per-test timeouts.** No test is timing out; the file is slow in aggregate, not blocked on a cap.
**Trimming the sandbox copy to fund more shards.** At 35.8 MB the copy is affordable once per shard; the cost that multiplies is small next to the work it parallelises.
The file's own per-test timing still does not exist in the packet, so the split between process chains and resets in finding 4 is inferred from counts rather than measured seconds.
**Renaming the file to a glob match.** It would break the loud-failure guarantee that the exact path provides.
**Sharding the cli lane in parallel with native `--shard`.** It would leave the heavy file whole and, per the existing runner's header, risks harness-owned failures from shared temp roots.
**Using `npm run test:sharded` for the cli lane.** It shards by file and runs shards serially, so it neither splits the heavy file nor shortens the lane's critical path.
No Vitest option splits one file's tests across workers; `describe.concurrent` is the only test-level concurrency, and iteration 6 ruled it out because the tests share a sandbox.

**`describe.concurrent` inside the file.** It would run 171 tests at once inside one worker against shared temp-dir bookkeeping, which is more concurrency than the file was written for and gains nothing over separate files.
**Moving the file without splitting it.** It would shorten the serial group but leave a 157 s block on one worker, which caps the suite's floor.
**Splitting fanout-run without moving it to the parallel project.** The serial project runs one file at a time, so four files would take the same wall time as one.
No per-describe timing exists, so the four-way split's balance is inferred from test counts rather than measured seconds.
**Claiming a saving from a summed metric.** Iterations 1 and 3 showed import is a sum over files, so the wall is the only number that proves a cut.
**Measuring under load.** The packet already recorded a false failure from a run under load; the baseline has to be quiet.
**One run as proof.** The packet's own three-run spread is 1.4%, so a single before/after pair cannot separate a real saving from noise without the 10% floor.
No CI wall-clock history exists, so the four-worker check is a proxy for `ubuntu-latest` rather than the real thing; a follow-up could record the first CI run's timing as the real baseline.
**Adding a third cut to the set.** Import sums and ledger caching are both off the critical path, and no other candidate survived eight iterations of checks.
**Presenting the totals as measured.** They are estimates built from measured baselines, and the protocol exists because that distinction matters.
**Reordering the cuts.** Cut A is smaller but cheaper to prove; Cut B is larger but needs a harness extraction. Either order works; Cut A first costs less if the operator stops after one.
No measurement can be taken inside this lineage's write surface, so the estimates cannot be upgraded to measurements here.
